sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.content: An AVL tree is a **binary search tree that rebalances itself**. After every insertion or deletion it checks the height of each subtree and rotates nodes so the tree never leans too far to one side.
items: **Balance factor (BF)**: height of the left subtree minus height of the right subtree
**AVL rule**: every node must have a BF of [[primary|-1, 0 or +1]]
A plain BST can degrade into a linked list; the AVL rule keeps the height at [[success|O(log n)]]
The same ordering rule as a BST still holds: left is smaller, right is larger

sections.heading: Rotations
sections.content: When a node's BF becomes +2 or -2, a rotation restores the balance without breaking the BST ordering.
items: **Right rotation (LL case)**: the left child becomes the new root of the subtree
**Left rotation (RR case)**: the right child becomes the new root of the subtree
**Left-right (LR) and right-left (RL)**: rotate the child first, then the node
Each rotation changes only a few pointers, so it takes [[success|O(1)]] time

sections.heading: Operation Complexity
sections.content: Because the height stays logarithmic, every operation stays fast even in the worst case.
items: **Search, insert, delete**: [[success|O(log n)]] in the worst case
An insertion needs **at most one rebalancing** (one or two rotations)
A deletion may rotate on **several levels** on the way up

sections.heading: Things to Watch
sections.content: AVL trees trade a little extra work on writes for predictable reads.
items: The tree is stricter than a red-black tree, so it **rotates more often** but is slightly shallower
Duplicate values are counted on the existing node, like the BST level
Turn auto-balance off to see how an AVL tree would degrade like a plain BST
